TR.22.notes: Richter prints three passages from this page (Reference Table: §§1189, 1332, 1493 = Tr. 2, the page number of Beltrami 1891, Tavola 1), in his order. The curator's reason names all three; lead 0 is set to the maxim because §1332 is, by Richter's own footnote, a contemporary poet's verse that Leonardo copied. Richter's footnote to §1493: Ammianus Marcellinus' histories were printed at Rome in 1474. The Gutenberg index file maps §1493 to the wrong text; the English here is taken from the Gutenberg text at the right place and read on the 1883 page.

it.text: Se'l Petrarca amò si forte il lauro, fu perch'egli è buon fralla salsiccia e tonno; io nō posso di lor ciancie far tesauro.

en.text: If Petrarch was so fond of bay, it was because it is of a good taste in sausages and with tunny; I cannot put any value on their foolery.

de.text: Wenn Petrarca den Lorbeer so sehr liebte, dann weil er gut zwischen Wurst und Thunfisch schmeckt; aus ihrem Geschwätz kann ich keinen Schatz machen.
de.label: Von einer KI aus dem gedruckten Text von Jean Paul Richter, 1883 übersetzt. Sie kann Fehler enthalten.

Richter's footnote: these lines are known to be by a contemporary poet (so he was told by Senatore Morelli), so Leonardo copied them rather than wrote them; Conte Porro read the last line 'I no posso di loro gia (sic) co' far tesauro'.

it.text: Qui fo ricordo di dimostrare la differentia ch'è dall'omo al cauallo, e similmente delli altri animali; e prima comincerò all'ossa, e proseguirò tutti li muscoli che sanza corde nascono e finiscono nelle ossa, e poi di quelli che cō corda nascono e finiscono nell'ossa, e poi di quelle che con una sola corda da v̄ canto.

en.text: Here I make a note to demonstrate the difference there is between man and the horse and in the same way with other animals. And first I will begin with the bones, and then will go on to all the muscles which spring from the bones without tendons and end in them in the same way, and then go on to those which start with a single tendon at one end.
en.label: Translation: Jean Paul Richter, 1883

de.text: Hier halte ich fest, dass ich den Unterschied zeigen will, der zwischen dem Menschen und dem Pferd besteht, und ebenso bei den anderen Tieren. Zuerst beginne ich mit den Knochen, dann gehe ich alle Muskeln durch, die ohne Sehnen an den Knochen entspringen und enden, dann die, die mit Sehne an den Knochen entspringen und enden, und dann die, die mit einer einzigen Sehne an einem Ende.
de.label: Von einer KI aus dem gedruckten Text von Jean Paul Richter, 1883 übersetzt. Sie kann Fehler enthalten.
doubts: The last clause has no verb in the Italian ('e poi di quelle che con una sola corda da v̄ canto'); Richter supplies 'start'. We leave it unfinished, as printed.
Richter's English passes over the middle clause ('e poi di quelli che cō corda nascono e finiscono nell'ossa', those that spring from and end in the bones with a tendon); our German keeps it.
'v̄': Richter's abbreviation for 'un'.

it.text: Il cavallo bianco si può ismachiare col ferretto di spagna o acqua forte overo col merdocco leuare il pelo nero al bianco cō rottorio, forzare a terra.

en.text: A white horse may have the spots removed with the spanish haematite or with aqua fortis or with . . . . Removes the black hair on a white horse with the singeing iron. Force him to the ground.
en.label: Translation: Jean Paul Richter, 1883

de.text: Ein weißes Pferd kann man mit spanischem Blutstein oder mit Scheidewasser oder mit Merdocco [?] von Flecken befreien. Das schwarze Haar am Weißen mit einem Ätzmittel [?] entfernen, zu Boden zwingen.
de.label: Von einer KI aus dem gedruckten Text von Jean Paul Richter, 1883 übersetzt. Sie kann Fehler enthalten.
doubts: 'merdocco': Richter leaves the word untranslated (his English has dots). We keep the word and mark it.
'rottorio': in older Italian a caustic that breaks the skin; Richter reads 'singeing iron'. We write 'Ätzmittel' and mark it.
'forzare' is printed in smaller type than the rest of the line; Richter gives no reason here. Read as 'force (him) to the ground', as Richter does.
Where 'overo col merdocco' belongs is open: we follow Richter and read it with the first sentence.

A.135.notes: Ravaisson's page heading (the editor's): 'PROPORTIONS DU VISAGE'. His notes: (1) the second paragraph belongs to the small face seen from the front at the right of the page, and the profile at the left also shows squares; (2) from the third paragraph on the lines apply to the young man's profile, with the letters placed so: a behind the head, b between the eyebrows, c at the hairline above the forehead, d at the tip of the chin, e at the parting of the hair behind, h at the neck, k where the underside of the chin meets the throat, n at the middle of the nose, p at the mouth, q at the jawbone, r above the nostril, s at the ear hole, x behind, at the base of the skull, 4 above the upper eyelid, 5 below the lower eyelid. Passages 3 to 5 measure the profile head the curator names; the lead is the first of them. Italics in 'it' and 'fr' mark words Leonardo struck out. Page match checked: the plate above the transcription (archive.org viewer n285) shows the same leaf as the SET image.

en.text: The face makes a square within itself: its width runs from one end of the eyes to the other, and its height from the top end of the nose to the underside of the lower lip of the mouth. Then what remains above and below this square makes the height of one more such square.

Ravaisson's note 1 says these lines belong to the small face seen from the front at the right of the page.

en.text: The space between the eyes is as large as one eye. The ear falls over the middle of the neck, in profile. It is as far from 4 to 5 as from 5 to r.
en.label: Translated by AI from the printed text of Charles Ravaisson-Mollien, 1881 to 1891. It may contain errors.
doubts: 'quanda' is Leonardo's slip; Ravaisson prints his correction '[quanta e]' (as much as is) in the Italian, and the translations follow it.
'chade nel mezo delchollo' is literally 'falls in the middle of the neck'; it is read as the ear standing above the middle of the neck when the head is seen in profile.
The print breaks 'del-chollo' across two lines; it is joined here.

H.136.notes: Placement confirmed: both passages carry 'H.2 15b]' (Leonardo's own number 15 in the second part of MS H; the library's folio 63 verso); Richter's Bibliography (vol. II p. 487, H.2) lists '15b 694, 1316'; Ravaisson vol. VI prints both under Ms H 'FOLIO 63 [15] (verso)' with the notes '(Oiseau lâché, sur lequel se jettent aussitôt un chien et un oiseau de proie). J.-P. Richter, t. I, no 694' and 'Idem, t. II, no 1316' (https://archive.org/details/lesmanuscritsdel06lo/page/n77/mode/1up; the page is in red chalk by his note). Richter's footnote to 1316: 'Above this text is another note, also referring to liberty; see No. 694.' Given in the edition's order (§694 in vol. I, §1316 in vol. II), which is also their order on the page. Ravaisson prints one more note on this side, on sand moved by two light currents of water ('larena mossa da 2 lievi corsi dacqua ...'); Richter does not print it, and it is not in this record. The curator's reason names the drawing (the running youth, the bird leaving his hand, the dog), which is the emblem of §694; lead 0.

en.text: The goldfinch gives victuals to its caged young. Death rather than loss of liberty.

de.text: Der Stieglitz gibt seinen Jungen im Käfig Futter [?]. Lieber den Tod, als die Freiheit zu verlieren.
de.label: Von einer KI aus dem gedruckten Text von Jean Paul Richter, 1883 übersetzt. Sie kann Fehler enthalten.
doubts: 'la vittouaglia' (food, victuals) is Richter's reading; his own note gives the manuscript as 'calderigio da il arouialio'. Ravaisson reads the same words as 'ilcalderigio da iltortomalio a figlioli ingabiati' and translates 'le chardonneret donne le tithymale aux petits en cage' (spurge, a poisonous plant); his note quotes Richter's 'vittouaglia ... gives victuals' and points to the word 'tutto maglio [tortomaglio, utumaglio]' on folio 65 [17] recto. The German follows Richter's printed Italian and marks the word [?]; with Ravaisson's reading the goldfinch gives its caged young spurge.
'prima morte che perdere libertà': literally 'death first, rather than losing liberty'.
